acts.title: Two photographs of a market

tts: My photo is of a market. There is a man in the foreground cooking something. — Sorry, did you say “cooking”? — Yes. — That is a difference, then. My photo shows a market too, but I cannot see anyone cooking anything. And I do not think I can see any men either. They all seem to be women, wearing headscarves, or straw hats and brightly coloured dresses.

Mine is a mixture of men and women. What are they selling? My photo shows different fruit and vegetables. I can see a lot of bananas. — Mine are selling fruit and vegetables too, and lots of bananas. But I bet your sellers are not on the water.

I am not quite sure what you mean by “on the water”. — I mean they are in boats. — In boats? — You look a bit confused. It is a floating market. All the sellers are in boats on the river. — Oh, I see. No, mine are definitely on land.

acts.title: Why We See Colour
tts: Beau Lotto is a neuroscientist based at University College London, specializing in human perception.

Why would anyone want to study colour? The answer is that colour is the simplest thing your brain does. Even jellyfish see lightness and they do not even have a brain. If we could understand how we see colour, then what is true there has to be true everywhere else.

How do we see? We do not know. We do not really know how the brain takes sensory stimuli and turns it into the conscious perception we experience. One of the reasons is that we have been approaching the problem with the wrong assumptions.

Simply put, colour enables us to distinguish between surfaces we would not otherwise be able to distinguish between. If two surfaces reflect the same amount of light, then without colour they would look exactly the same lightness. But if one reflects more shortwave lengths than the other, they now appear different colours.

There are only four categories of colour: red, green, blue and yellow. Everything else is a combination. Orange is red and yellow. Purple is red and blue. Why do we see four? Again, nobody really knows.

items.q: Why does Lotto study colour?
o: Because it is the simplest thing the brain does
Because it is the most complex

items.q: What does colour enable us to do?
o: Distinguish between surfaces that reflect the same amount of light

items.q: How many categories of colour does he say there are?
o: Four: red, green, blue and yellow

items.q: What does he say about how we see?

acts.title: Why We See Colour
tts: Colour does not exist out there. Close your eyes and colour disappears. Light is not coloured. Colour is a physical manifestation of your brain — that is where colour lives.
Everything you see exists in your head, which is an amazing paradox, because what we see seems to be out in the world in front of us.
Your brain did not evolve to see absolutes. It evolved to see relationships, and more significantly to see what those relationships meant for your behaviour in the past.
Colour, like everything else, is seeing a meaning. It is not a cognitive meaning, but it is still a behavioural meaning.

The practical outcome is ultimately about getting people to see things differently. If you can give them the principles by which the brain sees differently at the level of colour, they may be able to apply those principles to other things — the way they make decisions.

acts.title: Two different failures, and two different repairs
rule: When a conversation stalls, one of two things has gone wrong: you did not hear the words, or you heard them and did not follow. English repairs these differently, and using the wrong repair sends the wrong message — asking somebody to repeat themselves when the problem is meaning makes them say the same thing louder.
points: Sorry, did you say…? / I didn’t quite catch that. / Could you say that again?
You heard but did not follow
I’m not quite sure what you mean by… Quote the exact phrase back.
So, are you saying that…? / Am I right in thinking that…? Both invite a yes or a correction.
Do you see what I mean? / You look a bit confused. The second is friendly, not rude.
Repeating the exact words in quotation marks is the single most useful move: it isolates the problem.
eg: Sorry, did you say “cooking”?
You did not hear one word.
I’m sorry, I didn’t quite catch that.
You did not hear the sentence.
I’m not quite sure what you mean by “on the water”.
You heard it; you did not follow it.
So, are you saying that they’re all in boats?
Checking your interpretation.
Am I right in thinking that it’s a floating market?
The same, more formal.
Do you see what I mean?
Checking the other person is with you.
You look a bit confused.
Noticing, and offering to explain.
Let me put that another way.
Offering a second attempt.
In other words, the sellers are in boats.
Restating plainly.
Sorry — when you say “market”, do you mean indoors?
Quoting and narrowing at once.
acts.careful: “What?” on its own is not rude in every language. In English it is, with anybody you do not know well. Sorry, did you say…? costs one extra second.

write.q: Describe a scene in about 200 words for somebody who cannot see it, as if they had to draw it from your description. Work from the foreground backwards. Use at least four noun phrases with two adjectives in the correct order, keep the sense verbs accurate, and finish with one thing you genuinely cannot tell from looking.
write.model:
In the foreground, slightly left of centre, there is a low wooden table with three empty glasses on it and one that is still half full. Somebody has folded a paper napkin into a triangle and left it under the full glass.

Behind the table, two men in dark padded jackets are standing rather than sitting, which is the first thing that makes the picture odd. Neither is looking at the other. One of them is holding a set of car keys.

The background is a long white counter with a large decorative mirror above it, and in the mirror you can see the street, a bus stop, and about six people waiting who have no idea they are in the photograph.

What I can’t tell is whether the two men are together. They are standing close enough to be, and facing wrongly for it. In other words, the whole picture is a question about eighty centimetres wide, and I have looked at it for two years without answering it.
